newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's 96/97 surplus seen at HK$20 bln - Price Waterhouse.
newsitem.headline: HK's 96/97 surplus seen at HK$20 bln - Price Waterhouse.

text.p: Hong Kong is forecast to post a budget surplus of some HK$20 billion for the 1996/97 fiscal year ending March 31, about 12.5 times the original official estimate of HK$1.6 billion, Price Waterhouse said on Friday.

"This incredible outturn is going to be due mainly to stamp duty on the stock exchange as well as the property market," Roderick Houng-Lee, the accounting firm's head of taxation, told a news conference.
Stamp duties from the stock and property markets would turn out higher than expected, he said. He did not give figures.

He estimated fiscal reserves as of March 31 to be HK$168.6 billion, excluding the Land Fund for the Special Administrative Region (SAR) government that will run Hong Kong after Britain hands back the territory to China on July 1.
Including the Land Fund, reserves would top HK$310 billion, he said.
The SAR government will inherit not only the fiscal reserves but also the Land Fund, in which half of the income from government property sales has been placed.

With a further HK$141.6 billion estimated to be transferred to the reserves from the Land Fund on July 1, total reserves should reach about HK$340 billion by the end of fiscal 1997/98, Price Waterhouse said in a statement.
Financial Secretary Donald Tsang will release 1996/97 financial figures on March 12 when he makes his speech on the 1997/98 budget, which straddles the handover.
Houng-Lee said he did not expect Tsang to make major changes in the transitional budget.
"We don't think he's going to do much in terms of fiscal measures," the tax specialist said. "I think the first reason is of course this is a transitional budget."
There was also little reason to raise taxes with a high 1996/97 surplus expected, or to cut taxes while the territory's tax system was still the most attractive in Asia, he added.
The firm predicted the government would raise personal allowances by 8.8 percent, slightly above the 1996 inflation rate of six percent, he said.
Price Waterhouse proposed a one-off tax rebate in view of the estimated 1996/97 surplus.

"Hong Kong can afford a one-off salaries tax rebate of, say, five percent of 1996/97 salaries tax, and giving something back in this way has the advantage of not narrowing our future tax base in the same way as would an above-inflation increase in personal allowances," Houng-Lee said.
But said he did not expect the government to take up the suggestion.
Houng-Lee said he expected the local economy to be robust in 1997/98, but declined to give figures.
"I think the economy is going to be relatively robust given the (economic) situation in China has settled down," he said.
Hong Kong benefits from China's economic development by acting as a stepping-stone for multinationals to enter China, and by providing services to firms operating in the country.
Hong Kong is also a major transhipment point for Chinese products -- mainly textiles, electronics and consumer goods.
